Ukraine launches nearly 1,200 drones at Russia as US-led talks will consider wider European security - The Boston Globe

A team of European diplomats will be sent to the next peace negotiations, as many of the continent's leaders remain wary of Russian maneuvering and Trump’s praise for Putin. FEATURED VIDEO --- --- More talks are planned as negotiators seek a breakthrough in peace efforts, according to US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. A team of diplomats from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and the European Union will be sent to the talks, said European Council President Antonio Costa after a meeting in Dublin. The session was dominated by European efforts to avoid being sidelined in the US-led negotiations. Kushner, who is also President Trump’s son-in-law, said Russia had agreed to include Europe in upcoming talks, after Moscow’s long insistence that the continent’s governments should be excluded because they supported Ukraine. Europe’s presence at the table will allow negotiators “to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner said on X. European leaders are wary of Russian maneuvering, as well as Trump’s praise for Putin and his administration’s sharp criticism of Europe. Advertisement --- --- The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Europe must insist on a ceasefire before taking the negotiations further — the opposite of what Putin demands. “If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us,” she said in Dublin. Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden insisted that Europe must take its fate into its own hands. “We cannot let neither the Americans nor the Russians decide about our future,” Frieden said. Moscow is aiming “to dismantle NATO and the post-Cold War European security architecture,” the Institute for the Study of War said in an assessment Thursday.

(Reuters: Mike Blake) Mounting speculation over an espionage plot against Jensen Huang and his multiple alleged affairs reached a tipping point on Friday, when the tech billionaire quit as Nvidia's CEO. The controversy centred around his relationship with Alice Huang, who US intelligence reportedly suspects to be a Chinese spy, before claims emerged he had another two extra-marital affairs. While Mr Huang's resignation puts an end to his long reign over Nvidia, questions about America's national security and the US president's knowledge of the whole saga remain. text:
Microsoft outage highlights risks of relying on a single technology provider

A global Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services, affecting businesses, government agencies, healthcare services and law enforcement across several countries. The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour. Story continues below this ad The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services. Microsoft has scrambled to recover services A series of posts by Microsoft 365 on X suggested its engineers struggled to get the problem under control for some time, drawing teasing from other companies and users alike. But the tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents. Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer. As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks. Story continues below this ad For Outlook, many users said they couldn’t send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday. By Friday morning in the U.S., Microsoft said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.” Still, it warned of potential intermittent access and ongoing delays. On Thursday, the company said it had “successfully restored” Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

And for this it's essential to have a team and to speak with only one voice,” Costa said. European leaders have been concerned that a US-backed process will leave them sidelined and Kyiv vulnerable as Moscow and Washington decide the fate of a conflict that has roiled the continent. Ukraine is eager for support from its European allies. It's reluctant to leave the talks solely in the hands of a US administration that has often seemed to lean toward Moscow’s views. Russia, for its part, does not want European countries involved in direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine’s military effort. European leaders also distrust US President Donald Trump to negotiate on their behalf after a series of tense standoffs over trade, Greenland and conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. “Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin. “There is no more US support.” “At the end of the day, we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans,” he said. 'They will have a voice' European leaders fear Russian President Vladimir Putin will press Trump to back a peace settlement that weakens not just Ukraine but broader European security. Putin has demanded NATO troops be pulled back from Russia’s borders and that no European forces be deployed in Ukraine. As envoys from Washington, Moscow and Kyiv met this week in Abu Dhabi, several European countries, including the UK, France and Germany, attended discussions nearby, but not the main talks.

text:
Travel chaos worsens as communications problem causes ground stop at all U.S. airports while European airlines reel from wave of bomb threats | Fortune

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.
He added that the issue will take some time to fix but that there is no threat of a terrorist attack. “This isn’t another 9/11,” he said. “This is a telecommunication outage.” Still, the massive disruption comes as airlines in Europe suffered a wave of phony bomb threats this week. While they all appeared to hoaxes, at least one flight was diverted to a military base in France. Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said Friday that Europe appeared to be facing “hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare.” Meanwhile, consumers are still grappling with the aftermath of a Microsoft outage that shut down email, collaboration and AI functions. The company said Friday it had no indication that the ground stop is related to its global outage. The National Weather Service also said there has been no disruption to its radar systems Friday, denying talk online that it had caused the FAA communications issue. But speculation swirled elsewhere. Just days before the ground stop, the FAA announced it would deploy an AI tool to help air-traffic controllers, though it’s not clear if that was a factor on Friday. The FAA last issued a nationwide ground stop in 2023, when files related to an alert system for pilots was unintentionally deleted. It delayed thousands of flights, but they resumed soon after the disruption. Earlier this year, flights at New York airports were halted when a contractor accidentally cut a fiber communications line in New Jersey.
